name: Types of Perceptual Processing
what: This subtopic covers the two contrasting types of perceptual processing: bottom-up processing, which is driven by incoming sensory data, and top-down processing, which is driven by prior knowledge, expectations, and schemas. It explains how both types operate and interact.
why: Distinguishing bottom-up from top-down processing is central to explaining how the same sensory stimulus can be perceived differently by different people, and why familiarity speeds up recognition.

items.title: I can define bottom-up processing and explain when it is used
items.what: Bottom-up processing occurs when perception is built entirely from incoming sensory information, moving from specific stimulus details to a general understanding. It is typically used when the stimulus is unfamiliar or complex.
items.why: Bottom-up processing is the perceptual starting point for new experiences; it ensures that novel stimuli are analysed on their own terms rather than forced into a familiar category that may not fit.
items.example: A student learning Japanese for the first time reads each character individually, building up meaning letter by letter without being able to rely on prior recognition.

items.title: I can define top-down processing and explain when it is used
items.what: Top-down processing occurs when prior knowledge and expectations guide perception, moving from general knowledge to specific stimulus details. It is typically used when the stimulus is familiar and less complex.
items.why: Top-down processing makes perception faster and more efficient for routine stimuli, but it also introduces the possibility of misperception when expectations do not match reality.
items.example: A fluent reader can understand a sentence even if some letters are smudged or missing, because their prior knowledge of English fills in the gaps.

items.title: I can explain the role of schemas in top-down processing
items.what: Schemas are the collections of basic knowledge about a concept or stimulus stored in memory. In top-down processing, incoming stimuli are matched to existing schemas so they can be quickly recognised and interpreted.
items.why: Schemas make perception efficient, but they can also cause misperception when a stimulus is ambiguous and the wrong schema is applied.
items.example: A child who has only seen Labrador dogs may apply their dog schema to a fox when they first see one, perceiving it as a type of dog because it matches enough features of their existing schema.

items.title: I can compare bottom-up and top-down processing using direction and type of information
items.what: Bottom-up processing moves from specific stimulus features to general meaning, and is used for unfamiliar or complex stimuli. Top-down processing moves from general prior knowledge to specific features, and is used for familiar or less complex stimuli.
items.why: Being able to compare these two types of processing precisely, including their directions and contexts, is essential for correctly applying them to scenarios in exam questions.
items.example: Seeing a word written in an unusual font requires bottom-up processing to decode each letter; reading the same word in a familiar font activates top-down processing based on pattern recognition.

items.title: I can explain how bottom-up and top-down processing work together in one scenario
items.what: Both types of processing often occur together. Bottom-up processing registers the raw sensory details of a stimulus, while top-down processing draws on past experience to interpret those details. The two interact continuously during perception.
items.why: In real-world perception, stimuli are rarely processed by only one type; understanding their interaction explains how we can simultaneously notice new details and apply existing knowledge.
items.example: After stubbing a toe on a table leg (bottom-up: pain signals register the hazard), a person later perceives that table leg as dangerous and walks more carefully around it (top-down: past experience guides future perception).
